bib.title: Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch), Chapter 2: Working with text data

question: How is raw text turned into the input-target token batches and embedding vectors a GPT-like LLM trains on?
contributions: Tokenization: regex word tokenizer, vocabulary, special tokens, then GPT-2 BPE via tiktoken.
Sliding-window input-target sampling with a PyTorch Dataset/DataLoader.
Token embedding layers and absolute positional embeddings producing the LLM input.

results.claim: The BPE tokenizer used for GPT-2, GPT-3 and the original ChatGPT model has a vocabulary of 50,257 tokens, with <|endoftext|> the largest ID.
results.quote:
has a total vocabulary size of 50,257, with <|endoftext|> be‐
ing assigned the largest token ID.

results.claim: <|endoftext|> gets token ID 50256 in the GPT-2 BPE tokenizer.
The largest GPT-3 model (175B) uses an embedding size of 12,288 dimensions.

results.claim: The simple regex tokenizer yields 4690 tokens on The Verdict (no whitespace).
results.setup: regex split on punctuation, -- and whitespace

results.claim: The word-level vocabulary of The Verdict has 1,130 unique tokens; 1,132 after adding <|endoftext|> and <|unk|>.
With the GPT-2 BPE tokenizer The Verdict encodes to 5145 tokens, more than the 4690 word-level tokens.
A small embedding layer (vocab 6, dim 3) has a 6x3 weight matrix and acts as a row lookup, equivalent to one-hot times matmul.
results.quote:
the weight matrix has six rows
and three columns

results.claim: Token plus positional embeddings for a batch of 8 sequences of 4 tokens at width 256 give an 8x4x256 tensor.
results.setup: vocab 50,257, output_dim 256, max_length 4, stride 4, batch 8, learned absolute positions

results.claim: Raschka says input sizes of at least 256 are common for LLM training (the demo uses 4).
results.quote: It is common to train LLMs with input sizes of at least 256.

limits: BPE is only described briefly; implementation is out of scope and tiktoken is used.
Demo corpus is a single short story (20,479 characters), not realistic scale.
Embedding weights here are random and untrained; training is deferred to chapter 5.
Retrieval-augmented generation and sentence embeddings are declared out of scope.
practices: Do not lowercase text, since capitalization helps the LLM tell proper nouns and sentence structure (Sec 2.2).
Whether to keep whitespace tokens depends on the application; keep them for whitespace-sensitive text such as Python code (Sec 2.2 note).
Insert <|endoftext|> between unrelated documents when concatenating training text (Sec 2.4).
Use a BPE tokenizer so unknown words split into subwords or characters instead of <|unk|> (Sec 2.5).
Set stride equal to the window size to use the data without overlap, since more overlap could lead to increased overfitting (Sec 2.6).
Use drop_last=True to drop a short final batch and prevent loss spikes (Listing 2.6).
Truncate input longer than the supported context length (Sec 2.8).
With padded batches use an attention mask so the pad token choice is inconsequential (Sec 2.4).
Batch size is a tradeoff and a hyperparameter: small batches use less memory but give noisier updates (Sec 2.6).

terms.definition: a mapping from discrete objects, such as words, images, or even entire documents, to points in a continuous vector space
builds its vocabulary by iteratively merging frequent characters into subwords and frequent subwords into words
token separating unrelated text sources; analogous to [EOS] and also used for padding in GPT
token for words not in the vocabulary (not used by GPT's BPE tokenizer)
the number of positions the inputs shift across batches in the sliding window
a unique embedding per position added to the token embedding; GPT models learn them during training
emphasis on the relative position or distance between tokens, helping generalise to unseen sequence lengths
